question.text:
You are evaluating the financial performance of two retail chains based on their profitability ratios: Chain A: Return on Assets (ROA) = 10%, Return on Equity (ROE) = 15% Chain B: Return on Assets (ROA) = 12%, Return on Equity (ROE) = 18%
Assuming Chain A and Chain B have the same equity multiplier, which chain has a higher net profit margin?

answer.text: Both chains have the same net profit margin
Cannot determine from the given data

explanation.text: The Logic: Under the standard DuPont framework, ROA = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover. With equal equity multipliers, the chain with the higher ROA has the higher margin-times-turnover product, but the split between net profit margin and asset turnover cannot be inferred from ROA and ROE alone. Without an asset-turnover value (or net profit margin) for either chain, the higher net profit margin cannot be uniquely identified — Chain B could have a higher margin and similar turnover, or similar margin and higher turnover. The Trap: Picking Chain B feels intuitive because it has the higher ROA and ROE, but that only proves a higher Margin × Turnover product, not a higher net profit margin. Picking Chain A or "same margin" ignores the ROA gap; the trap is treating a multi-variable identity as if it had a single variable. Note: Source — NISM-Series-XXI-A workbook (September 2025), pages 45, 49 and 52 on ROA/ROE interpretation. The checked pages do not provide asset-turnover or net-profit-margin inputs for these chains.
